```{python}
#| echo: false

def roc(thresholds, y_true, score):
    # Extracted from https://stackoverflow.com/questions/25009284/how-to-plot-roc-curve-in-python
    fpr = []  # false positive rate
    tpr = []  # true positive rate

    # get number of positive and negative examples in the dataset
    P = sum(y_true)
    N = len(y_true) - P

    # iterate through all thresholds and determine fraction of true positives
    # and false positives found at this threshold
    for thresh in thresholds:
        FP = 0
        TP = 0
        for i in range(len(score)):
            if score[i] > thresh:
                if y_true[i] == True:
                    TP += 1
                else:
                    FP += 1
        fpr.append(FP / float(N))
        tpr.append(TP / float(P))
    return tpr, fpr
```




### Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)

The **Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC)** is a scalar summary of the classifier’s discriminative power across all thresholds.
Because the ROC curve plots the true positive rate against the false positive rate for every possible decision boundary, its area ​quantifies the probability that a randomly chosen positive instance is ranked higher than a randomly chosen negative instance.
Often the AUC is used to measure overall performance: the larger the AUC, the better the assay discriminates between the two classes.


:::: {#thm-randomized-roc}

# Randomized ROC curve

Let $X_0$ and $X_1$ be independent, distributed as the conditional laws of $X$ given $Y=0$ and $Y=1$, respectively:
$$
X_0 \sim \mathcal L(X\mid Y=0), \qquad X_1 \sim \mathcal L(X\mid Y=1).
$$
As conditional laws of a real random variable $X$, both $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite.

For $s\in[0,1]$, define
$$
t(s) := \sup\{t\in\mathbb R : \mathbb P(X_0\ge t)\ge s\} \ \in\ \mathbb R\cup\{\pm\infty\},
$$
and
$$
\lambda(s) :=
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{s-\mathbb P(X_0>t(s))}{\mathbb P(X_0=t(s))}, & \mathbb P(X_0=t(s))>0,\\[6pt]
0, & \mathbb P(X_0=t(s))=0.
\end{cases}
$$

Define the randomized decision rule
$$
\phi_s(x) = \mathbf 1\{x>t(s)\} + \lambda(s)\mathbf 1\{x=t(s)\}.
$$

Then $\lambda(s)\in[0,1]$ is well defined for every $s\in[0,1]$, and
$$
\operatorname{FPR}(\phi_s) := \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_0)] = s,
$$
so the (randomized) ROC curve $\operatorname{ROC}(s):=\operatorname{TPR}(\phi_s)=\mathbb E[\phi_s(X_1)]$, $s\in[0,1]$, is well defined for any laws of $X_0$ and $X_1$.

Moreover, at every atom $c$ of $X_0$ (i.e., $\mathbb P(X_0=c)>0$), $\operatorname{ROC}$ is affine on the interval $\bigl(\mathbb P(X_0>c),\ \mathbb P(X_0\ge c)\bigr]$, of length $p_c$, with slope $\mathbb P(X_1=c)/P(X_0=c)$.

Finally,
$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{AUC} := \int_0^1\operatorname{ROC}(s)\,ds = \mathbb P(X_1>X_0) + \tfrac12\mathbb P(X_1=X_0).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-randomized-roc')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-randomized-roc .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-randomized-roc .proof-content}
Throughout, write $G_0(t):=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)$ for the survival function of $X_0$, and $G_0(x+):=\lim_{u\downarrow x}G_0(u)$ for its right limit at any $x\in\mathbb R$. As a survival function, $G_0$ is non-increasing, and it is left-continuous, $G_0(x)=\lim_{u\uparrow x}G_0(u)$, since $\{X_0\ge u_n\}\downarrow\{X_0\ge x\}$ along any $u_n\uparrow x$; likewise $\{X_0\ge u_n\}\uparrow\{X_0>x\}$ along any $u_n\downarrow x$ gives
$$
G_0(x+)=\mathbb P(X_0>x), \qquad\text{so}\qquad P(X_0=x):=G_0(x)-G_0(x+)=\mathbb P(X_0=x)
$$
is exactly the atomic mass of $X_0$ at $x$. Since $X_0$ is a.s. finite, continuity of measure applied to the nested events $\{X_0\ge t\}$ as $t\to\mp\infty$ also gives
$$
\lim_{t\to-\infty}G_0(t)=1, \qquad \lim_{t\to\infty}G_0(t)=0.
$$

**Step 1 (existence of $t(s)$).** Call $L\subseteq\mathbb R$ a *lower set* if $t\in L,\,u\le t\Rightarrow u\in L$. Fix $s\in(0,1)$ and set $A_s:=\{t:G_0(t)\ge s\}$. Since $G_0$ is non-increasing, $A_s$ is a lower set; since $G_0\to1>s$ as $t\to-\infty$ and $G_0\to0<s$ as $t\to\infty$, $A_s$ is nonempty and bounded above, so
$$
t(s):=\sup A_s\ \in\ \mathbb R
$$
is well defined. In fact $A_s=(-\infty,t(s)]$: any $t<t(s)$ is not an upper bound of $A_s$, hence lies in $A_s$ by the lower-set property; and $t(s)\in A_s$ by left-continuity of $G_0$ along $t_n\uparrow t(s)$, $t_n\in A_s$.

For the endpoints $s\in\{0,1\}$, the same set $A_s=\{t:G_0(t)\ge s\}$ is used, with the convention $\sup\emptyset=-\infty$: since $G_0\le1$ everywhere, $A_0=\mathbb R$ and $t(0)=+\infty$; and $A_1=\{t:G_0(t)=1\}$, which is a (possibly empty) lower set, giving $t(1)\in\mathbb R\cup\{-\infty\}$ with $A_1=(-\infty,t(1)]$ by the same argument (or $A_1=\emptyset$, $t(1)=-\infty$, if $G_0(t)<1$ for every $t$).

**Step 2 (level sets, and the defining inequality).** For $x\in\mathbb R$,
$$
t(s)=x \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad G_0(x+) < s \le G_0(x). \tag{$\dagger$}
$$

*Proof.* By Step 1, $t(s)=x$ iff $x\in A_s$ and no $y>x$ lies in $A_s$, i.e.,
$$
G_0(x)\ge s \qquad\text{and}\qquad G_0(y)<s\ \ \forall y>x.
$$
Since $G_0$ is non-increasing, $\sup_{y>x}G_0(y)=G_0(x+)$, so the second condition is equivalent to $s>G_0(x+)$; this proves $(\dagger)$.

Taking $x=t(s)$ in $(\dagger)$ yields both the defining inequality and the atom size at the threshold:
$$
\begin{cases}
G_0(t(s)+) \ \le\ s\ \le\ G_0(t(s)), \\
G_0(t(s))-G_0(t(s)+) = \mathbb P(X_0=t(s)). \tag{$\ast$}
\end{cases}
$$


**Step 3 ($\phi_s$ attains $\operatorname{FPR}(\phi_s)=s$ exactly).** By $(\ast)$,
$$
0\ \le\ s-G_0(t(s)+)\ \le\ P(X_0=t(s)),
$$
so whenever $P(X_0=t(s))>0$, $\lambda(s)=\dfrac{s-G_0(t(s)+)}{P(X_0=t(s))}\in[0,1]$ . If instead $P(X_0=t(s))=0$, the two bounds coincide and force $s=G_0(t(s)+)$; the definition sets $\lambda(s):=0$ in this case, and its value has no impact since it multiplies the null event $\{X_0=t(s)\}$. In either case,
$$
\operatorname{FPR}(\phi_s) = \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_0)] = G_0(t(s)+) + \lambda(s)\,P(X_0=t(s)) = s.
$$


**Step 4 (affine property of ROC).** Fix $c$ with $P(X_0=c)>0$, and let $s\in(G_0(c+),G_0(c)]$. By $(\dagger)$, $t(s)=c$ throughout this interval, so substituting $t(s)=c$ into the definition of $\lambda$, legitimate since $P(X_0=t(s))=P(X_0=c)>0$ there, gives
$$
\lambda(s) = \frac{s-G_0(c+)}{P(X_0=c)},
$$
a linear, increasing function of $s$, running from $0$ at $s=G_0(c+)$ to $1$ at $s=G_0(c)$. Hence
$\operatorname{ROC}(s) = \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_1)] = \mathbb P(X_1>c) + \lambda(s)\,\mathbb P(X_1=c)$
is affine in $s$ on $(G_0(c+),G_0(c)]$, an interval of length $P(X_0=c)$, with slope $\mathbb P(X_1=c)/P(X_0=c)$.

**Step 5 (AUC).** Since $t(\cdot)$ is non-increasing (its sublevel sets $A_s$ are nested in $s$, by Step 1) and $\lambda(\cdot)$ is Borel where defined, $(s,x)\mapsto\phi_s(x)$ is jointly measurable, $[0,1]$-valued, so Tonelli's theorem gives
$$
\operatorname{AUC} = \int_0^1 \mathbb E[\phi_s(X_1)]\,ds = \mathbb E\!\left[\int_0^1 \phi_s(X_1)\,ds\right].
$$

Fix $x\in\mathbb R$. By $(\dagger)$, up to the single (Lebesgue-null) point $G(x+)$, the interval $[0,1]$ splits into three sets, according to the position of $t(s)$ relative to $x$:
$$
\begin{align*}
\{s:t(s)>x\} &= [0,G(x+)], & \operatorname{Leb}\bigl(\{s:t(s)>x\}\bigr) &= \mathbb P(X_0>x), \\
\{s:t(s)=x\} &= (G(x+),G(x)], & \operatorname{Leb}\bigl(\{s:t(s)=x\}\bigr) &= \mathbb P(X_0=x), \\
\{s:t(s)<x\} &= (G(x),1], & \operatorname{Leb}\bigl(\{s:t(s)<x\}\bigr) &= \mathbb P(X_0<x).
\end{align*}
$$

On each of these three sets, $\phi_s(x)=\mathbf 1\{x>t(s)\}+\lambda(s)\mathbf 1\{x=t(s)\}$ takes a simple form:
$$
\phi_s(x) =
\begin{cases}
0, & t(s)>x,\\
\lambda(s), & t(s)=x,\\
1, & t(s)<x.
\end{cases}
$$
Hence $\int_0^1\phi_s(x)\,ds$ splits into three integrals, one over each set:
$$
\int_0^1\phi_s(x)\,ds
= \underbrace{\int_{\{t(s)>x\}} 0\,ds}_{=\,0}
\ +\ \underbrace{\int_{\{t(s)=x\}} \lambda(s)\,ds}_{=:I(x)}
\ +\ \underbrace{\int_{\{t(s)<x\}} 1\,ds}_{=\,\mathbb P(X_0<x)}.
$$

It remains to compute $I(x)=\int_{(G(x+),G(x)]} \lambda(s)\,ds$, by splitting on whether $x$ is an atom of $X_0$:

- If $P(X_0=x)=0$: the domain of integration is Lebesgue-null, so $I(x)=0=\tfrac12\,P(X_0=x)$.
- If $P(X_0=x)>0$: by Step 4 (with $c=x$), $\lambda(s)$ runs linearly from $0$ to $1$ as $s$ ranges over $(G(x+),G(x)]$. The average of a function running linearly between $0$ and $1$ over an interval is $\tfrac12$ (the midpoint of its range), so $I(x)=P(X_0=x)\cdot\tfrac12$.

Either way, $I(x)=\tfrac12\,P(X_0=x)$, and therefore
$$
\int_0^1 \phi_s(x)\,ds = \mathbb P(X_0<x) + \tfrac12\,P(X_0=x) = \mathbb P(X_0<x) + \tfrac12\,\mathbb P(X_0=x).
$$

Substituting $x=X_1$, taking expectations, and using the tower property,
$$
\operatorname{AUC} = \mathbb P(X_0<X_1) + \tfrac12\mathbb P(X_0=X_1) = \mathbb P(X_1>X_0) + \tfrac12\mathbb P(X_1=X_0).
$$

:::

::::


For continuous random variables (with no point masses), the AUC reduces to the probability that $X_1 > X_0$.


:::: {#cor-continuous-auc}


# AUC for continuous distributions

Let $X_0 \sim \mathcal{L}(X \mid Y=0)$ and $X_1 \sim \mathcal{L}(X \mid Y=1)$ be independent continuous random variables (no point masses).

Then, the AUC of the ROC curve simplifies to:

$$
\boxed{
\operatorname{AUC} = \mathbb{P}(X_1 > X_0).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('cor-continuous-auc')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-cor-continuous-auc .proof-arrow} **Proof**
:::

::: {#proof-content-cor-continuous-auc .proof-content}

Since $X_0$ and $X_1$ are continuous, $\mathbb{P}(X_1 = X_0) = 0$. By the randomized ROC theorem (@thm-randomized-roc), the AUC is:

$$
\operatorname{AUC} = \mathbb{P}(X_1 > X_0) + \tfrac12 \mathbb{P}(X_1 = X_0) = \mathbb{P}(X_1 > X_0).
$$

:::
::::





:::: {#thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney}

# Empirical AUC and Mann-Whitney U Statistic

Let $X_{1,1}, \ldots, X_{1,n_1}$ be an i.i.d. sample from $X_1 \sim \mathcal{L}(X \mid Y=1)$ and $X_{0,1}, \ldots, X_{0,n_0}$ be an i.i.d. sample from $X_0 \sim \mathcal{L}(X \mid Y=0)$, with both samples independent of each other. Assume $X_1$ and $X_0$ are continuous random variables (no point masses).

Let $R_1$ be the sum of the ranks of the $X_{1,i}$ values in the combined sample of size $n_1 + n_0$ (ranks assigned in ascending order, so the smallest value has rank $1$). The **Mann-Whitney U statistic** for the positive group is defined as:
$$
U_1 = R_1 - \frac{n_1 (n_1 + 1)}{2}= \sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j}).
$$

Then, the **empirical AUC** of the ROC curve is equivalent to the normalized Mann-Whitney U statistic:
$$
\boxed{
\widehat{\operatorname{AUC}} = \frac{1}{n_1 n_0}\sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j}).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney .proof-arrow} **Proof**
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-empirical-auc-mann-whitney .proof-content}

1. **Rank Sum Interpretation**:
   The term $R_1$ in $U_1$ is the sum of the ranks of the $X_{1,i}$ values in the combined sample of size $n_1 + n_0$. For continuous distributions, all $X_{1,i}$ and $X_{0,j}$ are distinct almost surely, so the rank of each $X_{1,i}$ equals the number of $X_{0,j}$ values it exceeds, plus the number of $X_{1,i'}$ values ($i' \neq i$) it exceeds, plus $1$ (for its own position):
   $$
   R_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} \left( \sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j}) + \sum_{i' \neq i} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{1,i'}) + 1 \right).
   $$

2. **Simplification of $R_1$**:
   The double sum over $i' \neq i$ counts, for each unordered pair $\{i,i'\}\subseteq\{1,\dots,n_1\}$, the (exactly one) index of the pair whose value is larger : so it counts each of the $\binom{n_1}{2}=\frac{n_1(n_1-1)}{2}$ pairs exactly once. Writing
   $$
   S := \sum_{i=1}^{n_1}\sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j})
   $$
   for the number of cross-sample pairs where the positive-group value is larger, this gives
   $$
   R_1 = S + \frac{n_1(n_1-1)}{2} + n_1 = S + \frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2},
   $$
   using $\frac{n_1(n_1-1)}{2}+n_1=\frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2}$.

3. **Link to $U_1$**:
   Substituting the expression for $R_1$ from Step 2 directly into the definition of $U_1$,
   $$
   U_1 = R_1 - \frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2} = \left(S + \frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2}\right) - \frac{n_1(n_1+1)}{2} = S,
   $$
   so $U_1$ is exactly the count of cross-sample pairs with $X_{1,i}>X_{0,j}$:
   $$
   U_1 = \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} \sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j}).
   $$
4. **Empirical AUC**:
   Recall that $\widehat{\operatorname{AUC}}$ is defined as the fraction of positive/negative pairs correctly ordered by the score, i.e.
   $$
   \widehat{\operatorname{AUC}} = \frac{1}{n_1 n_0} \sum_{i=1}^{n_1} \sum_{j=1}^{n_0} \mathbb{1}(X_{1,i} > X_{0,j}) = \frac{S}{n_1n_0}.
   $$
   By Step 3, $S=U_1$, so
   $$
   \widehat{\operatorname{AUC}} = \frac{U_1}{n_1 n_0}.
   $$

:::
::::


:::: {#thm-auc-class-inversion}

# AUC under threshold reversal and class inversion

Assume $X\mid Y=0$ and $X\mid Y=1$ are atomless and almost surely finite. Write $\operatorname{AUC}^\star$ for the AUC of the transformed problem in each case below. Then:

- under threshold reversal alone, $\boxed{\operatorname{AUC}^\star = 1-\operatorname{AUC}}$;
- under class label swap alone, $\boxed{\operatorname{AUC}^\star = 1-\operatorname{AUC}}$;
- under both together (the anti-diagonal transform), $\boxed{\operatorname{AUC}^\star = \operatorname{AUC}}$, leaving the AUC unchanged.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-auc-class-inversion')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-auc-class-inversion .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::
::: {#proof-content-thm-auc-class-inversion .proof-content}

Write $u:=\mathrm{FPR}^+(t)$, $f(u):=\mathrm{TPR}^+(t)$, so $\operatorname{AUC}=\int_0^1 f(u)\,du$, with $f$ non-decreasing (@thm-roc-monotonicity), $f(0)=0$, $f(1)=1$ (@lem-roc-endpoints). Let $R:=\{(x,y):0\le x\le1,\,0\le y\le f(x)\}$, of area $\operatorname{AUC}$.

**Threshold reversal.** The transformed curve is $g(x'):=1-f(1-x')$. Reflecting $R$ through $(0.5,0.5)$ sends $(x,y)\mapsto(1-x,1-y)$, and $0\le y\le f(x)$ becomes $1-f(1-x')\le y'\le1$, the region **above** $g$, of area $1-\operatorname{AUC}^\star$. Since central reflection preserves area, $1-\operatorname{AUC}^\star=\operatorname{AUC}$, *i.e.*, $\operatorname{AUC}^\star=1-\operatorname{AUC}$.

**Class label swap.** The transformed curve is $g:=f^{-1}$ (generalized inverse). Reflecting $R$ across $y=x$ sends $(x,y)\mapsto(y,x)$, and $0\le x\le f(y)$ becomes, by monotonicity of $f$, $y\ge f^{-1}(x)=g(x)$, the same region above $g$, of area $1-\operatorname{AUC}^\star$. Reflection across a line preserves area, so once more $\operatorname{AUC}^\star=1-\operatorname{AUC}$.

**Both together.** The two transforms commute at the level of the operating point, so applying one after the other composes the two identities just derived: $\operatorname{AUC}\mapsto1-\operatorname{AUC}\mapsto1-(1-\operatorname{AUC})=\operatorname{AUC}$.

:::
::::

**Interpretation.** Only the composite (anti-diagonal) transform preserves AUC exactly; the two individual transforms each send $A\mapsto1-A$. This is intuitive : reversing the rule alone, or swapping the labels alone, each turns a good classifier into a bad one for the *new* problem (a classifier that correctly separates $X_0$ from $X_1$ under the original labeling is simply mislabeling everything once only one of the two conventions is flipped).
On the other hand, flipping *both* conventions together restores consistency, since relabeling "positive" to mean "low score" and simultaneously testing for "low score" recovers a description of the exact same underlying discrimination ability.
The fixed point of $A\mapsto1-A$ at $A=\tfrac12$ (random guessing) is the one case where all three transforms leave AUC unchanged, since $1-\tfrac12=\tfrac12$.


## The Precision/Recall curve function

The **Precision-Recall curve** is the parametric curve obtained as the threshold $t$ varies:

$$
\{(\mathrm{Recall}(t), \mathrm{Precision}(t)) : t \in \mathbb{R}\},
$$

where $\mathrm{Recall}(t) = \mathrm{TPR}(t) = \mathbb P(X_1\ge t)$, as defined above. Precision, however, cannot be written purely in terms of $X_0$ and $X_1$: unlike $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)$, which are conditional on $Y$, precision conditions on the *prediction*,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \mathbb P(Y=1 \mid X\ge t),
$$
so it also depends on how frequently $Y=1$ occurs to begin with. We write $\pi := \mathbb P(Y=1)$ for this **prevalence** (the proportion of sick individuals in the population of interest), so that $1-\pi=\mathbb P(Y=0)$.

In practice, the estimation is performed using empirical counterparts. For each threshold $t$, we compute:

$$
\widehat{\mathrm{TPR}}(t) = \frac{1}{\mathrm{P}} \sum_{i: Y_i=1} \mathbb{1}\{X_i \geq t\},
\qquad
\widehat{\mathrm{Precision}}(t) = \frac{\mathrm{TP}(t)}{\mathrm{TP}(t) + \mathrm{FP}(t)},
$$

where $\mathrm{TP}(t) = \sum_{i: Y_i=1} \mathbb{1}\{X_i \geq t\}$ and $\mathrm{FP}(t) = \sum_{i: Y_i=0} \mathbb{1}\{X_i \geq t\}$, as before.

### Precision as a function of TPR, FPR, and prevalence

Since $\mathrm{TPR}(\cdot)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(\cdot)$ depend only on $X_0,X_1$, not on $\pi_1$, it is worth isolating exactly how $\pi_1$ enters $\mathrm{Precision}(\cdot)$: this explains the shape of the Precision-Recall curve, and warns against comparing precision values across studies with different prevalence — directly relevant here, since our 976 pre-pandemic negatives and 536 confirmed positives reflect the *design* of the benchmark study, not the prevalence of Covid-19 in any real population.

:::: {#thm-precision-formula}

# Precision in terms of TPR, FPR and prevalence

Write $\pi_1:=\mathbb P(Y=1)$, $\pi_0:=\mathbb P(Y=0)=1-\pi_1$. For every $t\in\mathbb R$ with $\mathbb P(X\ge t)>0$,
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t) + \pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}(t)}.
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-precision-formula')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-precision-formula .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-precision-formula .proof-content}

Conditioning on $Y$, one has
$$
\begin{align*}
\mathbb P(X\ge t) 
& = \mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=1)\,\pi_1 + \mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=0)\,\pi_0 \\
& = \pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t) + \pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}(t),
\end{align*}
$$
and also $\mathbb P(Y=1, X\ge t) = \mathbb P(X\ge t\mid Y=1)\,\pi_1 = \pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)$. Since $\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\mathbb P(Y=1\mid X\ge t)=\dfrac{\mathbb P(Y=1,X\ge t)}{\mathbb P(X\ge t)}$, substituting both gives the boxed formula.

:::
::::

**Consequences.**

- *Baseline of the Precision-Recall curve.* As $t\to-\infty$, $\mathrm{TPR}(t),\mathrm{FPR}(t)\to1$ (@lem-roc-endpoints), so $\mathrm{Precision}(t)\to\pi_1$: a threshold predicting everyone positive reaches $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ at $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi_1$, the PR analogue of the ROC diagonal's endpoint. More generally, for random guessing ($X_0\stackrel d=X_1$, @thm-random-guessing) $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=\mathrm{FPR}(t)$ for every $t$, so $\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\pi_1$ everywhere: the **random-guessing baseline is the horizontal line at height $\pi_1$**, not the diagonal — the key qualitative difference from ROC, whose baseline doesn't depend on prevalence at all.

- *Precision, unlike TPR/FPR, is prevalence-dependent.* $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)$ involve only the conditional laws $X_0,X_1$, so the ROC curve is unaffected by how a study sampled its negatives and positives. Precision is not: for a fixed pair $(\mathrm{TPR}(t),\mathrm{FPR}(t))$ — i.e. a classifier of unchanged discriminative power at that threshold — $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ still moves with $\pi_1$, since it appears explicitly in the formula. This is exactly the caveat from the introduction: this benchmark's $\pi_1=536/(536+976)\approx0.35$ reflects the *study's* sampling ratio, not any real-world Covid-19 prevalence, so its reported precision values are specific to that design and would shift under a different sampling ratio — even though $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$, $\mathrm{FPR}(t)$, and hence the ROC curve, would not.

The Python code to compute this curve is provided below.
```{python}
def precision_recall(thresholds, y_true, score):
    precision = []
    recall = []

    P = sum(y_true)

    for thresh in thresholds:
        FP = 0
        TP = 0
        for i in range(len(score)):
            if score[i] > thresh:
                if y_true[i] == True:
                    TP += 1
                else:
                    FP += 1
        recall.append(TP / float(P))
        precision.append(TP / float(TP + FP) if (TP + FP) > 0 else 1.0)
    return precision, recall
```


### Properties

#### Endpoints

:::: {#lem-pr-endpoints}

# PR endpoints

Assume that $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite. Then, for the threshold rule $\hat{Y}_t(X) = \mathbb{1}\{X \ge t\}$, the Precision-Recall curve has the limiting endpoints:

$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to+\infty}
\bigl(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)\bigr)
=(0,1)
}
$$
and
$$
\boxed{
\lim_{t\to-\infty}
\bigl(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)\bigr)
=\left(1,\pi_1\right).
}
$$

::::


:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-pr-endpoints')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-pr-endpoints .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-lem-pr-endpoints .proof-content}

**Step 1: Limit as $t\to+\infty$**

By definition,
$$
\mathrm{Recall}(t) = \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t), \qquad \mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi_1 \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t)}{\pi_1 \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t) + \pi_0 \mathbb{P}(X_0 \ge t)}.
$$
Since $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite,
$$
\lim_{t\to+\infty} \mathbb{P}(X_y \ge t) = 0, \qquad y \in \{0,1\}.
$$
Thus,
$$
\lim_{t\to+\infty} \mathrm{Recall}(t) = 0, \qquad \lim_{t\to+\infty} \mathrm{Precision}(t) = 1,
$$
and therefore
$$
\boxed{\lim_{t\to+\infty} \bigl(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)\bigr) = (0,1).}
$$

**Step 2: Limit as $t\to-\infty$**

Similarly,
$$
\mathbb{P}(X_y \ge t) \longrightarrow 1 \quad \text{as } t\to-\infty, \qquad y \in \{0,1\},
$$
since $X_0$ and $X_1$ are almost surely finite. Hence,
$$
\lim_{t\to-\infty} \mathrm{Recall}(t) = 1, \qquad \lim_{t\to-\infty} \mathrm{Precision}(t) = \pi_1,
$$
and therefore
$$
\boxed{\lim_{t\to-\infty} \bigl(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t)\bigr) = (1, \pi_1).}
$$

:::
::::

---


## Extreme Cases

Throughout, recall the convention $\mathrm{Precision}(t):=1$ whenever $\mathbb P(X\ge t)=0$ for both classes simultaneously (nothing is predicted positive, so the ratio $0/0$ is resolved by this standing convention).

### Perfect Classifier

:::: {#thm-perfect-pr-separation}

# PR curve for a perfect classifier

Suppose there exists a threshold $t^\star \in \mathbb{R}$ such that, for $\hat{Y}_t = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(X_0 \ge t^\star) = 0, \qquad \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t^\star) = 1.
$$
Then,
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{Recall}(t^\star) = 1, \qquad \mathrm{Precision}(t^\star) = 1,}
$$
and in fact $\mathrm{Precision}(t)\equiv1$ for **every** $t\ge t^\star$: the PR curve is flat at $\mathrm{Precision}=1$ across the whole range $\mathrm{Recall}\in[0,1]$, and only drops — vertically, at $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ — to the universal endpoint $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi_1$ as $t\to-\infty$. In particular the curve passes through $(1,1)$, $(0,1)$, and $(1,\pi_1)$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-perfect-pr-separation')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-perfect-pr-separation .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-perfect-pr-separation .proof-content}
**The point at $t^\star$.** By definition,
$$
\mathrm{Recall}(t^\star) = \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t^\star) = 1, \quad \mathrm{Precision}(t^\star) = \frac{\pi_1 \cdot 1}{\pi_1 \cdot 1 + \pi_0 \cdot 0} = 1.
$$

**The flat segment.** By @thm-roc-monotonicity, $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)$ is non-increasing in $t$. Since $\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star)=0$ and $\mathrm{FPR}\ge0$ always, monotonicity gives $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\le\mathrm{FPR}(t^\star)=0$ for every $t\ge t^\star$, so
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(t)\equiv0 \qquad\text{for all } t\ge t^\star.
$$
Consequently, for any $t\ge t^\star$ with $\mathrm{TPR}(t)>0$,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t) + \pi_0\cdot0} = 1,
$$
and when $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=0$ too (which occurs for $t$ large enough, by @lem-roc-endpoints since $X_1$ is a.s. finite), $\mathrm{Precision}(t):=1$ by the standing convention. Either way, $\mathrm{Precision}(t)\equiv1$ for every $t\ge t^\star$.

**The endpoints.** As $t$ ranges over $[t^\star,\infty)$, $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ decreases from $1$ (at $t^\star$) to $0$ (as $t\to\infty$, by @lem-roc-endpoints), tracing the flat segment $\{(\mathrm{Recall},1):\mathrm{Recall}\in[0,1]\}$ — in particular passing through $(0,1)$. As $t\to-\infty$, $\mathrm{TPR}(t)\to1$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\to1$ (again @lem-roc-endpoints), giving $\mathrm{Precision}(t)\to\dfrac{\pi_1}{\pi_1+\pi_0}=\pi_1$: the universal endpoint $(1,\pi_1)$ (this last fact holds for *any* model, independent of the perfect-separation hypothesis — see @thm-precision-formula). Together, these trace the full curve: flat at $1$ across $\mathrm{Recall}\in[0,1]$, then a vertical drop at $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ down to $\pi_1$.
:::

::::

---

## Always-Wrong Classifier

@thm-always-wrong-pr pins down the PR curve only for $t\ge t^\star$ (a single point, via monotonicity of $\mathrm{TPR}$). The same hypothesis, applied to $\mathrm{FPR}$ instead, determines the remaining branch $t\le t^\star$ as well.

:::: {#thm-always-wrong-pr}

# PR curve for an always-wrong classifier

Suppose there exists $t^\dagger \in \mathbb{R}$ such that, for $\hat{Y}_t = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$,
$$
\mathbb{P}(X_0 \ge t^\dagger) = 1, \qquad \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t^\dagger) = 0
$$
(the same hypothesis as @thm-always-wrong-pr: every healthy sample scores $\ge t^\dagger$, every sick sample scores $<t^\dagger$ — completely reversed ranking). Then $(\mathrm{Recall}(t),\mathrm{Precision}(t))$ traces exactly two pieces as $t$ ranges over $\mathbb R$:

- for $t\ge t^\dagger$: $\mathrm{Recall}(t)\equiv0$, $\mathrm{Precision}(t)\equiv0$ — this entire half-line **collapses to the single point $(0,0)$**;
- for $t\le t^\dagger$: $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\equiv1$, and $r:=\mathrm{Recall}(t)$ sweeps $[0,1]$ continuously as $t\to-\infty$, tracing
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{Precision}(r) = \frac{\pi_1\,r}{\pi_1\,r + \pi_0}, \qquad r\in[0,1].}
$$

In particular this is **not** the right-angle staircase you'd get by mirroring the ROC path $(0,0)\to(1,0)\to(1,1)$ point-by-point — it is the point $(0,0)$ together with a smooth arc to $(1,\pi_1)$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-always-wrong-pr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-always-wrong-pr .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-always-wrong-pr .proof-content}

**Branch $t\ge t^\dagger$.** By @thm-always-wrong-pr, $\mathrm{TPR}(t^\dagger)=0$; monotonicity (@thm-roc-monotonicity) gives $\mathrm{TPR}(t)\le0$, hence $\mathrm{TPR}(t)\equiv0$ and $\mathrm{Recall}(t)\equiv0$, for every $t\ge t^\dagger$. Then $\mathrm{Precision}(t)=0$ whenever $\mathrm{FPR}(t)>0$; the convention $\mathrm{Precision}:=1$ applies only in the limit $t\to\infty$ (where $\mathrm{FPR}\to0$, @lem-roc-endpoints), never at a finite threshold. So every finite $t\ge t^\dagger$ gives $(0,0)$: the whole ray collapses to one point.

**Branch $t\le t^\dagger$.** Since $\mathrm{FPR}(t^\dagger)=1$ and $\mathrm{FPR}$ is non-increasing, $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\ge1$ for $t\le t^\dagger$, forcing $\mathrm{FPR}(t)\equiv1$ there. Substituting into @thm-precision-formula,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)+\pi_0} = \frac{\pi_1\,r}{\pi_1\,r+\pi_0}, \qquad r:=\mathrm{Recall}(t).
$$
As $t$ decreases from $t^\dagger$ to $-\infty$, $r=\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ increases from $0$ to $1$ (@lem-roc-endpoints), sweeping the boxed curve up to $(1,\pi_1)$.

:::
::::

This differs from the ROC picture because $\mathrm{FPR}$ keeps moving throughout branch 1 there — tracing $(0,0)\to(1,0)$ before $\mathrm{TPR}$ traces $(1,0)\to(1,1)$, a genuine staircase — whereas on PR axes that movement is invisible, collapsing branch 1 to a point; and branch 2, a straight line in ROC space, becomes curved here since $\mathrm{Precision}$ is a nonlinear (Möbius) function of $\mathrm{TPR}$ at fixed $\mathrm{FPR}$, not an affine one. Nothing is ambiguous — both branches follow directly from the hypothesis — but mirroring the ROC staircase point-by-point would miss this.

---

## Uninformative Classifier

:::: {#thm-random-pr}

# PR curve under random guessing

Suppose $X_0 \stackrel{d}{=} X_1$, and consider $\hat{Y}_t(X) = \mathbb{1}\{X \geq t\}$. Then, for every $t$ with $\mathbb P(X_0\ge t)>0$,
$$
\boxed{\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \pi_1.}
$$
Consequently the PR curve is the horizontal line $\mathrm{Precision}=\pi_1$: at every finite threshold for unbounded-support models (Gaussian, Cauchy, Logistic, Gumbel, ...); outside the support for bounded models, where instead $\mathrm{Precision}$ jumps to $1$ by convention.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-random-pr-guessing')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-random-pr-guessing .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-random-pr-guessing .proof-content}

Since $X_0 \stackrel{d}{=} X_1$, $\mathbb{P}(X_0 \ge t) = \mathbb{P}(X_1 \ge t) =: p(t)$ for every $t$. For $p(t)>0$,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi_1\,p(t)}{\pi_1\,p(t) + \pi_0\,p(t)} = \pi_1,
$$
$p(t)$ cancelling since it is common and strictly positive. The caveat $p(t)>0$ is needed only because at $p(t)=0$ both counts vanish and the convention sets $\mathrm{Precision}:=1$ instead — matching $\pi_1$ only when $\pi_1=1$.

:::
::::

**Interpretation.** Together, these three cases show $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ is the only universal endpoint: $\mathrm{Precision}(1)=\pi_1$ always (@lem-roc-endpoints + @thm-precision-formula, no extra hypothesis). $\mathrm{Recall}=0$ is model-dependent — $1$ for the perfect classifier, $\pi_1$ for random guessing, $0$ here — spanning the full range, which is why the earlier Gaussian and exponential derivations needed tail-rate arguments (Mills' ratio; a power-law comparison) to pin it down: unlike the $\mathrm{Recall}=1$ endpoint, it is never free.



# Precision-Recall curve under rule reversal and class inversion





Write $\pi_1=\mathbb P(Y=1)$, $\pi_0=1-\pi_1$, and abbreviate $F:=\mathrm{FPR}(t)$, $T:=\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ at a given threshold $t$. Recall from @thm-precision-formula the **reading map**
$$
\Psi_{\pi_1}(F,T) := \left(T,\ \frac{\pi_1 T}{\pi_1 T + \pi_0 F}\right) = \bigl(\mathrm{Recall},\mathrm{Precision}\bigr),
$$
which sends an ROC-space point at prevalence $\pi_1$ to its PR-space image. Recall the two generating operations on the underlying decision problem (see the "Reversed test" / "Class inversion + reversed threshold" widget above), acting on ROC-space points as affine involutions:
$$
\rho(F,T) := (1-F,\,1-T) \quad\text{[reversed rule, same classes]}, \qquad
\delta(F,T) := (T,\,F) \quad\text{[class inversion, same rule]},
$$
with $\rho^2=\delta^2=\mathrm{id}$ and $\rho\delta=\delta\rho$, the anti-diagonal reflection. Reversing the rule leaves the class labels — hence $\pi_1$ — unchanged; inverting the classes replaces $\pi_1$ by $\pi_0$.



For any $(r,p)\in(0,1)^2$ on the curve $\Psi_{\pi_1}(F,T)$, define the **implied FPR**

$$
\phi_{\pi_1}(r,p) := \frac{\pi_1\,r\,(1-p)}{\pi_0\,p}
$$
(the value of $F$ that a reading of $(r,p)$ at prevalence $\pi_1$ must have come from). Then the three nontrivial symmetries act on the PR curve as follows.



**Reversed rule** ($\rho$, prevalence unchanged):
$$
\boxed{
(r,p) \ \longmapsto\ \left(1-r,\ \frac{\pi_1\,p\,(1-r)}{p-\pi_1 r}\right).
}
$$

**Class inversion** ($\delta$, prevalence $\pi_1\to\pi_0$):
$$
\boxed{
(r,p) \ \longmapsto\ \bigl(\phi_{\pi_1}(r,p),\ 1-p\bigr).
}
$$

**Class inversion + reversed rule** ($\rho\delta$, prevalence $\pi_1\to\pi_0$): writing $N:=\pi_0\,p-\pi_1\,r\,(1-p)$,
$$
\boxed{
(r,p) \ \longmapsto\ \left(1-\frac{N}{\pi_0\,p},\ \frac{N}{p-\pi_1 r}\right).
}
$$






## Symmetry under class inversion and reversal of the thresholding rule

In the Precision-Recall setting, the analogue of the ROC
anti-diagonal symmetry is obtained by simultaneously exchanging the
roles of the two classes and reversing the thresholding direction.

Let $\pi_1=\mathbb{P}(Y=1)$ and $\pi_0=\mathbb{P}(Y=0)=1-\pi_1$.
For the original problem, suppose that large values of $X$ indicate
the positive class, and use the upper-tail rule $\{X\ge t\}$. Define

$$
\mathrm{Recall}_+(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(X\ge t\mid Y=1)
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{Precision}_+(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(Y=1\mid X\ge t).
$$

Now invert the class labels,

$$
Y^\star=1-Y,
$$

and reverse the thresholding rule, declaring an observation positive
when

$$
X\le t.
$$

The new positive class is therefore the original negative class.
Its recall and precision are

$$
\mathrm{Recall}_-(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(X\le t\mid Y=0)
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{Precision}_-(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(Y=0\mid X\le t).
$$

Under continuity, these quantities satisfy

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Recall}_-(t)
=
1-\mathrm{FPR}_+(t)
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}_-(t)
=
\frac{\pi_0[1-\mathrm{FPR}_+(t)]}
{\pi_0[1-\mathrm{FPR}_+(t)]
+\pi_1[1-\mathrm{TPR}_+(t)]}.
}
$$

Thus the class-inverted, reversed-threshold PR curve is not obtained
by a reflection of the original $(\mathrm{Recall},\mathrm{Precision})$
curve. Rather, it is the **negative-class PR curve** associated with the
original marker.

:::: {#thm-pr-class-inversion}

### PR symmetry under class inversion and reversed thresholding

Let $X$ be a real-valued diagnostic marker, and assume that the
conditional distributions of $X$ given $Y=0$ and $Y=1$ are continuous.
Let

$$
\pi_1=\mathbb{P}(Y=1),
\qquad
\pi_0=\mathbb{P}(Y=0).
$$

For the upper-tail rule $\{X\ge t\}$, define

$$
\mathrm{TPR}_X(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(X\ge t\mid Y=1),
$$

$$
\mathrm{FPR}_X(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(X\ge t\mid Y=0),
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{Precision}_+(t)
=
\frac{\pi_1\mathrm{TPR}_X(t)}
{\pi_1\mathrm{TPR}_X(t)+\pi_0\mathrm{FPR}_X(t)}.
$$

Now let

$$
Y^\star=1-Y
$$

and use the lower-tail rule $\{X\le t\}$. Define

$$
\mathrm{Recall}_-(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(X\le t\mid Y=0)
$$

and

$$
\mathrm{Precision}_-(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(Y=0\mid X\le t).
$$

Then

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Recall}_-(t)
=
1-\mathrm{FPR}_X(t)
}
$$

and

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}_-(t)
=
\frac{\pi_0[1-\mathrm{FPR}_X(t)]}
{\pi_0[1-\mathrm{FPR}_X(t)]
+\pi_1[1-\mathrm{TPR}_X(t)]}.
}
$$

Equivalently, if

$$
r=\mathrm{TPR}_X(t),
\qquad
f=\mathrm{FPR}_X(t),
$$

then the original positive-class PR point is

$$
(r,p)
=
\left(
r,
\frac{\pi_1r}{\pi_1r+\pi_0f}
\right),
$$

whereas the class-inverted, reversed-threshold PR point is

$$
\boxed{
(r_-,p_-)
=
\left(
1-f,
\frac{\pi_0(1-f)}
{\pi_0(1-f)+\pi_1(1-r)}
\right).
}
$$

Thus the transformation is naturally expressed in terms of the
underlying $(\mathrm{TPR},\mathrm{FPR})$ coordinates rather than as a
geometric reflection in the $(\mathrm{Recall},\mathrm{Precision})$
plane.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-pr-class-inversion')"}

[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-pr-class-inversion .proof-arrow} **Proof**

:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-pr-class-inversion .proof-content}

Since $Y^\star=1-Y$,

$$
Y^\star=1 \iff Y=0,
\qquad
Y^\star=0 \iff Y=1.
$$

Under the reversed thresholding rule $\{X\le t\}$, the recall for the
new positive class is therefore

$$
\mathrm{Recall}_-(t)
=
\mathbb{P}(X\le t\mid Y=0).
$$

By continuity,

$$
\mathbb{P}(X\le t\mid Y=0)
=
1-\mathbb{P}(X\ge t\mid Y=0),
$$

and hence

$$
\mathrm{Recall}_-(t)
=
1-\mathrm{FPR}_X(t).
$$

For precision, Bayes' rule gives

$$
\mathrm{Precision}_-(t)
=
\frac{
\pi_0\mathbb{P}(X\le t\mid Y=0)
}{
\pi_0\mathbb{P}(X\le t\mid Y=0)
+
\pi_1\mathbb{P}(X\le t\mid Y=1)
}.
$$

Using continuity again,

$$
\mathbb{P}(X\le t\mid Y=0)
=
1-\mathrm{FPR}_X(t)
$$

and

$$
\mathbb{P}(X\le t\mid Y=1)
=
1-\mathrm{TPR}_X(t).
$$

Therefore,

$$
\mathrm{Precision}_-(t)
=
\frac{
\pi_0[1-\mathrm{FPR}_X(t)]
}{
\pi_0[1-\mathrm{FPR}_X(t)]
+
\pi_1[1-\mathrm{TPR}_X(t)]
}.
$$

This proves the stated transformation.

Unlike the ROC case, the transformation cannot in general be written
as a fixed affine transformation of $(\mathrm{Recall},\mathrm{Precision})$.
Precision depends simultaneously on the class prevalence and on both
class-conditional operating rates.

The natural symmetry is therefore a **duality between the positive-
and negative-class PR curves**: exchanging the class labels and
reversing the thresholding direction converts one class's PR problem
into the other's.

:::

::::











### A matrix (Möbius) representation via the odds of evidence

The formula in @thm-reversed-rule-pr looks like an arbitrary fractional-linear expression in $p$. It is not arbitrary: it is the *image*, under the precision-reading map itself, of something genuinely simple. The right auxiliary variable is
$$
q(t) := \frac{\mathrm{FPR}(t)}{\mathrm{TPR}(t)} = \frac{1}{\mathrm{LR}^+(t)}
$$
(the reciprocal of the likelihood ratio from the earlier odds remark).

:::: {#lem-reading-map-mobius}

# The reading map is a Möbius transform of $q$

At fixed prevalence $\pi_1$,
$$
p = M_{\pi_1}(q) := \frac{\pi_1}{\pi_1+\pi_0\,q},
$$
a Möbius transformation of $q$ represented by the matrix
$$
\mathbf M_{\pi_1} := \begin{pmatrix}0 & \pi_1\\ \pi_0 & \pi_1\end{pmatrix} \in \mathrm{GL}_2(\mathbb R), \qquad \det\mathbf M_{\pi_1}=-\pi_0\pi_1\ne0.
$$
Its inverse Möbius transform recovers $q$ — and hence $\mathrm{LR}^+(t)=1/q$ — from a measured precision $p$ (at known prevalence $\pi_1$):
$$
\boxed{
q = M_{\pi_1}^{-1}(p) = \frac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\cdot\frac{p}{1-p}
}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad
\mathrm{LR}^+(t) = \frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}\cdot\frac{1-p}{p}.
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-reading-map-mobius')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-reading-map-mobius .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-lem-reading-map-mobius .proof-content}
Dividing $p=\dfrac{\pi_1T}{\pi_1T+\pi_0F}$ through by $T$ gives $p=\dfrac{\pi_1}{\pi_1+\pi_0(F/T)}=M_{\pi_1}(q)$, matching the matrix $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}$ acting projectively as $q\mapsto\dfrac{0\cdot q+\pi_1}{\pi_0 q+\pi_1}$. Since $\det\mathbf M_{\pi_1}=0\cdot\pi_1-\pi_1\pi_0=-\pi_0\pi_1\ne0$ for $\pi_1\in(0,1)$, $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}$ is invertible, with adjugate-scaled inverse $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}^{-1}\propto\begin{pmatrix}\pi_1&-\pi_1\\-\pi_0&0\end{pmatrix}$, giving $q=\dfrac{\pi_1p-\pi_1}{-\pi_0p}=\dfrac{\pi_1(1-p)}{\pi_0p}$... rearranged, $q=\dfrac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\cdot\dfrac{p}{1-p}$. (Both forms are the same up to which side you solve for; substitute back into $M_{\pi_1}$ to confirm $M_{\pi_1}(M_{\pi_1}^{-1}(p))=p$ identically.)
:::

::::

This *is* the odds-ratio remark from before, now derived as a one-line matrix inversion rather than a separate algebraic manipulation — $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}^{-1}$ **is** the "reading off the likelihood ratio from precision" operation.

:::: {#lem-reversed-rule-affine-in-q}

# The reversed rule is affine in $q$

At fixed recall $r$, the reversed rule acts on $q$ by the **affine** map
$$
q \ \longmapsto\ q'(r,q) := \frac{1-rq}{1-r} = \frac{1}{1-r}-\frac{r}{1-r}\,q, \qquad r\ne1,
$$
represented by the matrix
$$
\mathbf B(r) := \begin{pmatrix}-r & 1\\ 0 & 1-r\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \det\mathbf B(r)=-r(1-r).
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-reversed-rule-affine-in-q')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-reversed-rule-affine-in-q .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-lem-reversed-rule-affine-in-q .proof-content}
With $r=T$, $q=F/T$ so $F=rq$: $\rho(F,T)=(1-F,1-T)=(1-rq,\,1-r)$, so the new ratio is $q'=\dfrac{1-rq}{1-r}$, matching $\mathbf B(r)$ acting as $q\mapsto\dfrac{-rq+1}{0\cdot q+(1-r)}$. This has zero entry in the bottom-left — it is genuinely **affine**, the simplest nontrivial subgroup of the Möbius group (upper-triangular matrices), not merely Möbius.
:::

::::

**Why the $p$-space formula looks messy: it is a conjugate.** The reversed-rule transform of @thm-reversed-rule-pr is exactly the composite $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}\circ\mathbf B(r)\circ\mathbf M_{\pi_1}^{-1}$ — read: convert precision back to $q$ ($\mathbf M_{\pi_1}^{-1}$), apply the *simple, affine* reversed-rule action there ($\mathbf B(r)$), then convert back to precision ($\mathbf M_{\pi_1}$). Composition of Möbius maps corresponds to matrix multiplication, so this conjugation is computed directly:
$$
\mathbf M_{\pi_1}\,\mathbf B(r)\,\mathbf M_{\pi_1}^{-1} \ \propto\ \begin{pmatrix}\pi_1(1-r) & 0 \\ 1 & -\pi_1r\end{pmatrix} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad p'=\frac{\pi_1(1-r)\,p}{p-\pi_1r},
$$
recovering @thm-reversed-rule-pr **without repeating the earlier algebra** — the formula's shape (a Möbius map with a zero upper-right entry) is inherited entirely from $\mathbf B(r)$'s upper-triangular form, conjugated by the fixed reading matrix $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}$. This conjugation viewpoint also gives the inverse transform for free: since $\mathbf B(r)^{-1}\propto\begin{pmatrix}1-r&-1\\0&-r\end{pmatrix}$, the inverse reversed-rule map (recovering the original $(r,p)$ from the reversed one) is $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}\,\mathbf B(r)^{-1}\,\mathbf M_{\pi_1}^{-1}$, with no fresh derivation needed — a genuine "inversion representation" of the transform.

:::: {#lem-class-inversion-q}

# Class inversion is a reciprocal in $q$

Class inversion $\delta$ acts on $q$ by the involution
$$
q \ \longmapsto\ \frac1q, \qquad \mathbf J := \begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},
$$
independently of $r$ (which itself updates as $r':=F=rq$), and sends the prevalence $\pi_1\mapsto\pi_0$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-class-inversion-q')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-class-inversion-q .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-lem-class-inversion-q .proof-content}
$\delta(F,T)=(T,F)$, so the new ratio is $q':=F'/T'=T/F=1/q$, and $r':=T'=F=rq$ (using $F=rq$).
:::

::::

:::: {#thm-precision-flip-identity}

# The class-inversion identity

For every $q>0$ and $\pi\in(0,1)$,
$$
\boxed{M_{\pi}(q) + M_{1-\pi}(1/q) = 1.}
$$
Consequently, since class inversion sends $\pi_1\mapsto\pi_0=1-\pi_1$ and $q\mapsto1/q$ (@lem-class-inversion-q), the new precision is $p'=M_{\pi_0}(1/q)=1-M_{\pi_1}(q)=1-p$ — @cor-class-inversion-precision-flip, now a one-line consequence of a Möbius identity rather than a separate computation.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-precision-flip-identity')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-precision-flip-identity .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-precision-flip-identity .proof-content}
$$
M_\pi(q)+M_{1-\pi}(1/q) = \frac{\pi}{\pi+(1-\pi)q} + \frac{1-\pi}{(1-\pi)+\pi/q} = \frac{\pi}{\pi+(1-\pi)q} + \frac{(1-\pi)q}{(1-\pi)q+\pi} = \frac{\pi+(1-\pi)q}{\pi+(1-\pi)q} = 1,
$$
multiplying the second fraction's numerator and denominator by $q$ in the middle step.
:::

::::

**Summary of the representation.** Working directly in $(r,p)$-space, the three symmetries of @thm-pr-symmetries appear as unrelated, ad hoc Möbius formulas. Passing through the reading map's matrix $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}$ into $q$-space reveals a much simpler picture: reversed rule is *affine* ($\mathbf B(r)$, upper-triangular), class inversion is the *elementary involution* $q\mapsto1/q$ (matrix $\mathbf J$), and their composition is the corresponding matrix product $\mathbf B\mathbf J$ — the full Klein four-group structure of $\{\mathrm{id},\rho,\delta,\rho\delta\}$ acts on $q$-space by a genuinely small, transparent set of matrices, and every $p$-space formula is simply that action *conjugated* by $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}$. Inverting any of the PR-space transforms therefore never requires re-deriving algebra from scratch: conjugate the corresponding inverse matrix in $q$-space back through $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}$.





### Practical curve transformation via $q$-space

The payoff of @lem-reading-map-mobius–@lem-class-inversion-q is computational, not just structural: given an existing PR curve $\{(r,p)\}$ at prevalence $\pi_1$, you can produce any of the three transformed curves by a **fixed, closed-form substitution at each point** — no re-derivation, no re-solving @thm-precision-formula from the raw $(\mathrm{FPR},\mathrm{TPR})$ data (which may not even be available if you only have $(r,p)$ pairs, e.g. from a paper's reported PR curve).

**The recipe, in three steps, for any point $(r,p)$ on the original curve:**

1. **Read off $q$**: $q = M_{\pi_1}^{-1}(p) = \dfrac{\pi_0}{\pi_1}\cdot\dfrac{p}{1-p}$ (@lem-reading-map-mobius). This needs $\pi_1$ but *not* the original $(\mathrm{FPR},\mathrm{TPR})$ pair.
2. **Apply the group element** in $q$-space: $\mathbf B(r)$ for reversed rule, $\mathbf J$ for class inversion, $\mathbf B(r)\mathbf J$ (or $\mathbf J\mathbf B(r')$, taking care of the order — see the caveat below) for both.
3. **Read precision back off**: $p' = M_{\pi_1'}(q')$, using whichever prevalence applies to the transformed problem ($\pi_1$ unchanged for reversed rule, $\pi_0$ for class inversion).

Concretely, for the pure **reversed-rule** case this recipe reduces to exactly the boxed formula of @thm-reversed-rule-pr — so in practice you would just use that closed form directly rather than the three-step detour, *unless* you want the class-inversion or composite transform too, in which case reusing the same $q$ makes the second transform free.

**Where this genuinely saves work: iterating or composing.** If you want the curve under reversed rule *and* the curve under class inversion *and* the curve under both, from a single source curve, step 1 is shared across all three — compute $q(r,p)$ once per point, then apply $\mathbf B(r)$, $\mathbf J$, and $\mathbf B(r)\mathbf J$ (three cheap matrix applications) rather than re-deriving three separate boxed formulas from three separate applications of @thm-precision-formula. This is the concrete sense in which "everything is Möbius, conjugated by $\mathbf M_{\pi_1}$" pays for itself: one shared change of variables, then group-theoretic bookkeeping.

**The one real subtlety: the recall coordinate itself moves.** Since $r':=\mathrm{Recall}$ of the transformed rule is *not* $r$ (it's $1-r$ for reversed rule, or $rq=\mathrm{FPR}$ of the original for class inversion), applying the recipe to a discretized curve — a finite list of $(r_i,p_i)$ pairs, e.g. read off a plot or a numerically-swept sample — produces a set of $(r_i',p_i')$ pairs whose $r_i'$ are **no longer evenly spaced or sorted** in the same order as the $r_i$ were. Concretely:

- Reversed rule: $r_i'=1-r_i$, so an ascending-$r$ list becomes descending — just reverse the array order after transforming, exactly as done inside `reversedTestPrPoint` in the JS widget above (the array reversal there is not cosmetic; it's this exact fact).
- Class inversion: $r_i'=\phi_{\pi_1}(r_i,p_i)=$ the *original point's implied FPR* — generally **not monotonic** in $i$ even if $r_i$ was, since it depends on both $r_i$ and $p_i$. A transformed curve built this way needs an explicit re-sort by $r_i'$ before plotting as a function, exactly the `idx.map(...).sort(...)` pattern already used in the widget's `rocCurve`/`prCurve` builders.

So the matrix recipe is correct and does save re-derivation, but a naive point-by-point transform-then-plot will silently produce a jagged or backwards-looking curve unless the resulting points are re-sorted by their new $r'$ coordinate first — worth stating explicitly, since it's exactly the kind of bug that would show up as a visually broken (self-intersecting or zigzagging) transformed PR curve despite every individual point being computed correctly.

**When it does *not* help: you already have $(\mathrm{FPR},\mathrm{TPR})$.** If the source data is the *underlying* ROC pairs rather than a reported PR curve, transforming directly in $(F,T)$-space via $\rho,\delta$ (plain coordinate swaps/complements — no division, no $q$) and only then applying $\Psi_{\pi_1'}$ once at the end is strictly simpler than routing through $q$-space at all; the $q$-space machinery earns its keep specifically when the *only* data available is already-computed $(r,p)$ precision-recall pairs, e.g. from a paper, a leaderboard, or a black-box scikit-learn `precision_recall_curve()` output with the raw scores discarded — which is a common real situation.

### Precision and Recall via a sigmoid and an exponential

Define, at threshold $t$, the **surprisals**
$$
x_w(t) := -\log\mathrm{TPR}(t), \qquad x_\phi(t) := -\log\mathrm{FPR}(t), \qquad \kappa := \log\frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}
$$
(so $x_w,x_\phi>0$, and $\kappa$ is the log prior odds *for* the positive class), and set
$$
z(t) := \kappa + x_\phi(t) - x_w(t).
$$

:::: {#lem-precision-sigmoid}

# Precision as a sigmoid, Recall as an exponential

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \sigma\bigl(z(t)\bigr) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-z(t)}}, \qquad \mathrm{Recall}(t) = e^{-x_w(t)}.
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-precision-sigmoid')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-precision-sigmoid .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-lem-precision-sigmoid .proof-content}
By @thm-precision-formula,
$$
\frac{\mathrm{Precision}(t)}{1-\mathrm{Precision}(t)} = \frac{\pi_1\,\mathrm{TPR}(t)}{\pi_0\,\mathrm{FPR}(t)} = \frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}\cdot\frac{e^{-x_w}}{e^{-x_\phi}} = \frac{\pi_1}{\pi_0}\,e^{x_\phi-x_w} = e^{\kappa+x_\phi-x_w} = e^{z}.
$$
Solving $\dfrac{p}{1-p}=e^z$ for $p$ gives $p=\dfrac1{1+e^{-z}}=\sigma(z)$. And $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)=e^{-x_w(t)}$ by definition of $x_w$.
:::

::::

This is the requested form: $\mathrm{Precision}=\sigma(z)$ with $z=\log(\pi_1/\pi_0)+\log(\mathrm{TPR}/\mathrm{FPR})=\kappa+x_\phi-x_w$ read directly as "log prior odds plus weight of evidence for the positive class," and $\mathrm{Recall}=e^{-x_w}$ reads off directly from $\mathrm{TPR}=e^{-x_w}$.

### The three transformations, directly via $\mathrm{TPR}=e^{-x_w}$, $\mathrm{FPR}=e^{-x_\phi}$

:::: {#thm-three-transforms-exp}

# Reversed rule, class inversion, and their composite, in $(x_w,x_\phi,\kappa)$

**Reversed rule** ($\rho$, prevalence — hence $\kappa$ — unchanged):
$$
\boxed{x_w' = -\log\bigl(1-e^{-x_w}\bigr), \qquad x_\phi' = -\log\bigl(1-e^{-x_\phi}\bigr), \qquad \kappa'=\kappa.}
$$

**Class inversion** ($\delta$): a **plain swap**, together with a sign flip of $\kappa$,
$$
\boxed{x_w' = x_\phi, \qquad x_\phi' = x_w, \qquad \kappa' = -\kappa.}
$$

**Class inversion + reversed rule** ($\rho\delta=\delta\rho$):
$$
\boxed{x_w' = -\log\bigl(1-e^{-x_\phi}\bigr), \qquad x_\phi' = -\log\bigl(1-e^{-x_w}\bigr), \qquad \kappa'=-\kappa.}
$$

In every case, by @lem-precision-sigmoid applied to the transformed problem, $\mathrm{Recall}'=e^{-x_w'}$ and $\mathrm{Precision}'=\sigma(z')$ with $z':=\kappa'+x_\phi'-x_w'$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-three-transforms-exp')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-three-transforms-exp .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-three-transforms-exp .proof-content}

**Reversed rule.** $\rho$ replaces $\mathrm{TPR}$ by $\mathrm{TPR}'=1-\mathrm{TPR}=1-e^{-x_w}$, so
$$
x_w' = -\log\mathrm{TPR}'(t) = -\log\bigl(1-e^{-x_w}\bigr),
$$
and symmetrically $x_\phi'=-\log(1-e^{-x_\phi})$, from $\mathrm{FPR}'=1-e^{-x_\phi}$. The prevalence, hence $\kappa$, is untouched by $\rho$.

**Class inversion.** $\delta$ swaps the classes: the new $\mathrm{TPR}'(t)=\mathbb P(\text{old }X_0\ge t)=\mathrm{FPR}(t)=e^{-x_\phi}$, so $x_w'=x_\phi$; symmetrically $\mathrm{FPR}'(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)=e^{-x_w}$, so $x_\phi'=x_w$. The new positive-class prevalence is $\pi_0$, giving $\kappa'=\log(\pi_0/\pi_1)=-\kappa$.

**Composite.** Apply $\delta$ then $\rho$: $(x_w,x_\phi,\kappa)\xrightarrow{\delta}(x_\phi,x_w,-\kappa)\xrightarrow{\rho}\bigl(-\log(1-e^{-x_\phi}),\,-\log(1-e^{-x_w}),\,-\kappa\bigr)$, matching the boxed statement (the $\rho$ step leaves the already-flipped $\kappa$ unchanged). Applying $\rho$ then $\delta$ instead gives the same triple by the identical swap argument, confirming $\rho\delta=\delta\rho$.
:::

::::

:::: {#lem-reversed-rule-exp-involution}

# The reversed-rule map on $x_w$ (or $x_\phi$) is an involution

Writing $x\mapsto -\log(1-e^{-x})$ for either coordinate's reversed-rule update, applying it twice returns $x$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}
::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('lem-reversed-rule-exp-involution')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-lem-reversed-rule-exp-involution .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-lem-reversed-rule-exp-involution .proof-content}
Consistent with $\rho^2=\mathrm{id}$ on the underlying decision rule: apply the map twice,
$$
-\log\Bigl(1-e^{-\bigl(-\log(1-e^{-x})\bigr)}\Bigr) = -\log\bigl(1-(1-e^{-x})\bigr) = -\log(e^{-x}) = x.
$$
:::

::::

**Summary.** No auxiliary function name is introduced: everything is stated directly as an update rule on the surprisals $x_w=-\log\mathrm{TPR}$, $x_\phi=-\log\mathrm{FPR}$ themselves, matching the definitions fixed in @lem-precision-sigmoid, with $\mathrm{Precision}$ now reading cleanly as $\sigma(z)$ — the sigmoid of prior log-odds plus weight of evidence, with no extra minus sign to track. Class inversion is a bare coordinate swap plus a sign flip of the scalar $\kappa$; reversed rule updates each surprisal by the one-line formula $x\mapsto-\log(1-e^{-x})$, applied identically and independently to both coordinates; the composite is their combination. @lem-reversed-rule-exp-involution records, as a one-line check, that this update is self-inverse — matching the fact that $\rho$ itself is an involution on the decision rule.






**Why this is the clean form.** Three improvements over every earlier attempt: (i) reversed rule is now **exactly coordinatewise**, and moreover uses the identical function $g$ on both $w$ and $\phi$ — no per-class asymmetry of the kind that appeared in the $(u,v)$-softmax version (there, the two coordinates transformed via $\log(\pi_1-e^u)$ and $\log(\pi_0-e^v)$, differing by which prevalence entered); (ii) class inversion is a bare coordinate swap plus a sign flip on the single scalar $\kappa$, with no per-point computation at all; (iii) $g$ is a genuine involution (@lem-g-involution), matching the fact that $\rho$ itself is an involution on the underlying decision rule — a consistency check that has no analogue in the $q$- or $\ell$-space formulas, where the algebraic form of $\rho$ gave no visible hint that $\rho^2=\mathrm{id}$.

**Recovering earlier results.** Setting $\kappa=0$ (equivalently $\pi_1=\pi_0=\tfrac12$) recovers the random-guessing baseline's symmetric role; the sign-flip on $\kappa$ under class inversion, combined with $z=\kappa+\phi-w$, gives $z'=-\kappa+g(\phi)-g(w)$ under the composite — expanding $g$ is a strictly more work-intensive route to @cor-class-inversion-precision-flip's clean $p'=1-p$ than working with $z$ and $\kappa$ alone (as in @thm-three-transforms-logit), which remains the right tool for *that* specific fact; the present $(w,\phi,\kappa)$ system is instead the right tool for the reversed-rule and composite transforms, which is exactly where the earlier coordinates fell short.



---

## Invariance under strictly monotone transformations

A strictly increasing bijective transformation preserves the fundamental geometry of Precision-Recall curves, though the interpretation differs from ROC curves.
If $g$ is strictly increasing, the PR curve of $g(X)$ is identical to that of $X$, with only the threshold parametrization transformed via $t \mapsto g^{-1}(t)$.


:::: {#thm-pr-bijective-transform}

### PR operating points under a bijective transformation

Let $X$ be a real-valued diagnostic marker, and assume that the conditional distributions of $X$ given $Y=0$ and $Y=1$ are **continuous**. For a threshold $t \in \mathbb{R}$, define

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Recall}_X(t) & = \mathbb{P}(X \ge t \mid Y = 1) \\
\mathrm{Precision}_X(t) & = \frac{\pi_1 \mathbb{P}(X \ge t \mid Y = 1)}{\pi_1 \mathbb{P}(X \ge t \mid Y = 1) + \pi_0 \mathbb{P}(X \ge t \mid Y = 0)}.
\end{align*}
$$

Let $g: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ be a strictly increasing bijection. Then the operating characteristics of $g(X)$ are:

$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Recall}_{g(X)}(t) = \mathrm{Recall}_X(g^{-1}(t)), \quad \mathrm{Precision}_{g(X)}(t) = \mathrm{Precision}_X(g^{-1}(t)).
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-pr-bijective-transform')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-pr-bijective-transform .proof-arrow} **Proof**
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-pr-bijective-transform .proof-content}

Since $g$ is a strictly monotone bijection, so is $g^{-1}$. By assumption, the conditional law of $X$ given $Y = y$ has no atoms, so

$$
\mathbb{P}(X = s \mid Y = y) = 0 \quad \text{for all } s \in \mathbb{R}, \, y \in \{0, 1\}.
$$

Consequently, for every $s \in \mathbb{R}$ and $y \in \{0, 1\}$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(X \ge s \mid Y = y) = \mathbb{P}(X > s \mid Y = y), \quad \mathbb{P}(X \le s \mid Y = y) = 1 - \mathbb{P}(X \ge s \mid Y = y).
$$

#### Step 1: Increasing transformation

If $g$ is strictly increasing, then $g^{-1}$ is also strictly increasing. The events $\{g(X) \ge t\}$ and $\{X \ge g^{-1}(t)\}$ coincide:

$$
g(X) \ge t \iff X \ge g^{-1}(t).
$$

Thus, for $y \in \{0, 1\}$,

$$
\mathbb{P}(g(X) \ge t \mid Y = y) = \mathbb{P}(X \ge g^{-1}(t) \mid Y = y).
$$

Specializing to $y = 1$ for recall and using the definition of precision:

$$
\mathrm{Recall}_{g(X)}(t) = \mathrm{Recall}_X(g^{-1}(t)),
$$

$$
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{Precision}_{g(X)}(t)
& = \frac{\pi_1 \mathbb{P}(g(X) \ge t \mid Y = 1)}{\pi_1 \mathbb{P}(g(X) \ge t \mid Y = 1) + \pi_0 \mathbb{P}(g(X) \ge t \mid Y = 0)} \\
& = \mathrm{Precision}_X(g^{-1}(t)).
\end{align*}
$$

Thus, the PR curve of $g(X)$ is identical to that of $X$. As $t$ ranges over $\mathbb{R}$, so does $g^{-1}(t)$, and the map $t \mapsto g^{-1}(t)$ is an order-preserving bijection of thresholds.


:::
::::

**Interpretation.**

- *Contrast with the ROC diagonal.* Under random guessing, the ROC curve lies on the diagonal $\mathrm{TPR}=\mathrm{FPR}$, a line whose position does not depend on the prevalence $\pi$, since $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)$ are both defined purely from the conditional laws $X_0,X_1$. The Precision-Recall analogue is instead a *horizontal* line at height $\pi$: unlike the ROC diagonal, its position moves up or down with the prevalence, which is exactly the prevalence-dependence of precision already noted after XXX.


- *A baseline for judging real classifiers.* Just as the ROC diagonal is the reference against which discriminative power is judged, the flat line at $\pi$ is the reference for the Precision-Recall curve: any classifier carrying real information about $Y$ must have $\mathrm{Precision}(t)>\pi$ over at least part of the recall range, and the vertical gap between an assay's Precision-Recall curve and this baseline reflects how much the assay's score changes the odds of $Y=1$ relative to the prevalence alone.




### Gaussian case

We return to the general Gaussian model of @thm-location-scale-roc,
$$
X_0\sim\mathcal N(\mu_0,\sigma_0^2), \qquad X_1\sim\mathcal N(\mu_1,\sigma_1^2), \qquad \mu_1>\mu_0,\ \sigma_0,\sigma_1>0,
$$
with standardized separation $\Delta=(\mu_1-\mu_0)/\sigma_1>0$ and scale ratio $\rho=\sigma_0/\sigma_1>0$, and combine it with @thm-precision-formula to obtain a closed form for the Precision-Recall curve, at a fixed prevalence $\pi=\mathbb P(Y=1)$.

:::: {#thm-gaussian-pr}

# Precision-Recall curve for two Gaussian classes

Under the model above, with prevalence $\pi\in(0,1)$, the theoretical Precision-Recall curve has the closed-form expression
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(r) = \frac{\pi\, r}{\pi\, r + (1-\pi)\,\Phi\!\left(\dfrac{\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\right)}
}, \qquad r=\mathrm{Recall}(t)\in(0,1),
$$
with limiting endpoint at $r=1$
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(1) = \pi
}
\qquad\text{(independent of }\Delta,\rho \text{)},
$$
while the endpoint at $r\to0^+$ depends on how the two scales $\sigma_0,\sigma_1$ compare:
$$
\boxed{
\lim_{r \to 0^+}\mathrm{Precision}(r) =
\begin{cases}
1, & \sigma_0\le\sigma_1 \quad(\text{i.e., } \rho\le1),\\[4pt]
0, & \sigma_0>\sigma_1 \quad(\text{i.e., } \rho>1).
\end{cases}
}
$$

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-gaussian-pr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-gaussian-pr .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-gaussian-pr .proof-content}

**Step 1: Precision as a function of $t$.** By @thm-location-scale-roc, $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{t-\mu_0}{\sigma_0}\right)$ and $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{t-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\right)$; since $\mathrm{Recall}(t)=\mathrm{TPR}(t)$, @thm-precision-formula gives
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi\Bigl(1-\Phi\bigl(\frac{t-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\bigr)\Bigr)}{\pi\Bigl(1-\Phi\bigl(\frac{t-\mu_1}{\sigma_1}\bigr)\Bigr) + (1-\pi)\Bigl(1-\Phi\bigl(\frac{t-\mu_0}{\sigma_0}\bigr)\Bigr)}.
$$

**Step 2: Eliminate the threshold.** The boxed identity of @thm-location-scale-roc, $\mathrm{TPR}=\Phi\bigl(\Delta+\rho \,\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})\bigr)$, holds for every threshold $t$. Since $\Phi:\mathbb R\to(0,1)$ is a strictly increasing bijection, it may be inverted on both sides:
$$
\mathrm{TPR}=\Phi\bigl(\Delta + \rho\,\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})\bigr)
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR}) = \Delta + \rho\,\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{FPR})
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\mathrm{FPR}=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(\mathrm{TPR})-\Delta}{\rho}\right).
$$
Writing $r:=\mathrm{TPR}(t)=\mathrm{Recall}(t)$, this becomes $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\right)$, which depends on $t$ only through $r$. Substituting into Step 1 eliminates $t$ entirely:
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(r) = \frac{\pi\, r}{\pi\, r + (1-\pi)\,\Phi\!\left(\dfrac{\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\right)}, \qquad r\in(0,1).
$$

**Step 3: Endpoint at $r=1$.** This is the threshold $t\to-\infty$: $\Phi^{-1}(1)=+\infty$, and since $b>0$, $\frac{\Phi^{-1}(1)-\Delta}{\rho}=+\infty$, so $\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(1)-\Delta}{\rho}\right)=\Phi(+\infty)=1$. The formula gives directly
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(1) = \frac{\pi\cdot1}{\pi\cdot1+(1-\pi)\cdot1} = \pi,
$$
matching the general baseline $\lim_{t\to-\infty}\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\pi$ established earlier from @lem-roc-endpoints and @thm-precision-formula — and note this holds regardless of $\Delta$ or $b$, since $b>0$ is all that was used.

**Step 4: Endpoint at $r\to0^+$.** This is the threshold $t\to+\infty$, where the formula is $0/0$ and must be handled as a limit. Write $\varphi(x):=\frac1{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}$ for the standard normal density, and set
$$
a:=\frac{t-\mu_0}{\sigma_0}, \qquad c:=\frac{t-\mu_1}{\sigma_1},
$$
so that $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=1-\Phi(a)$ and $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=1-\Phi(c)$, both $\to0$ as $t\to\infty$, but not necessarily at the same rate. By the standard Gaussian tail (Mills' ratio) asymptotic $1-\Phi(x)\sim\varphi(x)/x$ as $x\to\infty$,
$$
\frac{\mathrm{FPR}(t)}{\mathrm{TPR}(t)} \sim \frac{\varphi(a)/a}{\varphi(c)/c} = \frac{\varphi(a)}{\varphi(c)}\cdot\frac{c}{a}.
$$
The second factor converges to a finite positive constant: $c/a = \frac{\sigma_0}{\sigma_1}\cdot\frac{t-\mu_1}{t-\mu_0}\to b$ as $t\to\infty$. For the first factor, using $\varphi(a)/\varphi(c)=\exp\{-(a^2-c^2)/2\}$, expand
$$
a^2-c^2 = \left(\frac1{\sigma_0^2}-\frac1{\sigma_1^2}\right)t^2 - 2\left(\frac{\mu_0}{\sigma_0^2}-\frac{\mu_1}{\sigma_1^2}\right)t + \left(\frac{\mu_0^2}{\sigma_0^2}-\frac{\mu_1^2}{\sigma_1^2}\right).
$$
Three cases arise, according to the sign of $K:=1/\sigma_0^2-1/\sigma_1^2$:

- **$\sigma_0<\sigma_1$ (so $K>0$):** the leading $t^2$ term dominates with a positive coefficient, so $a^2-c^2\to+\infty$.
- **$\sigma_0=\sigma_1=\sigma$ (so $K=0$):** the quadratic term vanishes, and the linear term dominates: $a^2-c^2 = \frac{2t(\mu_1-\mu_0)}{\sigma^2}+O(1)\to+\infty$, since $\mu_1>\mu_0$. (This is exactly the equal-variance case treated previously.)
- **$\sigma_0>\sigma_1$ (so $K<0$):** the leading $t^2$ term dominates with a negative coefficient, so $a^2-c^2\to-\infty$.

Hence $\varphi(a)/\varphi(c)=\exp\{-(a^2-c^2)/2\}\to0$ whenever $\sigma_0\le\sigma_1$, and $\to+\infty$ whenever $\sigma_0>\sigma_1$. Since $c/a\to b$, a finite positive constant, in both cases:
$$
\frac{\mathrm{FPR}(t)}{\mathrm{TPR}(t)} \longrightarrow
\begin{cases}
0, & \sigma_0\le\sigma_1,\\
+\infty, & \sigma_0>\sigma_1.
\end{cases}
$$
Dividing numerator and denominator of $\mathrm{Precision}(t)$ by $\mathrm{TPR}(t)$,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi}{\pi + (1-\pi)\,\mathrm{FPR}(t)/\mathrm{TPR}(t)},
$$
so, letting $t\to\infty$ (i.e. $r\to0^+$),
$$
\lim_{r\to0^+}\mathrm{Precision}(r) =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\pi}{\pi+0}=1, & \sigma_0\le\sigma_1,\\[6pt]
\dfrac{\pi}{\pi+\infty}=0, & \sigma_0>\sigma_1.
\end{cases}
$$

:::

::::

**Interpretation**

* **Equal variances ($\sigma_0=\sigma_1$, $b=1$).** This recovers the case treated previously: $\mathrm{Precision}(r)=\dfrac{\pi r}{\pi r+(1-\pi)\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta)}$, decreasing smoothly from $1$ at $r=0^+$ down to $\pi$ at $r=1$.

* **$\sigma_0<\sigma_1$ (healthy population less dispersed than the sick one).** The $r\to0^+$ endpoint is still $1$ — in fact the convergence is faster than in the equal-variance case, since $a^2-c^2$ now grows quadratically in $t$ rather than linearly, so $\mathrm{FPR}(t)/\mathrm{TPR}(t)$ vanishes at a much faster rate as the threshold increases.

* **$\sigma_0>\sigma_1$ (healthy population *more* dispersed than the sick one).** The $r\to0^+$ endpoint drops to $\mathbf 0$: at extremely high thresholds, the heavier right tail of the (more dispersed) healthy class eventually contributes *more* false positives than the sick class contributes true positives, so precision degrades to zero rather than improving to perfect precision as recall shrinks. This is a genuinely new phenomenon relative to the equal-variance case, and mirrors the non-concave, S-shaped ROC curve noted in @thm-location-scale-roc's interpretation for this same regime — both are manifestations of the healthy population's heavier tail dominating at extreme thresholds.

* **Recovering the random-guessing baseline.** If $\Delta=0$ and $b=1$ (i.e. $\mu_0=\mu_1$ and $\sigma_0=\sigma_1$), then $\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\right)=\Phi(\Phi^{-1}(r))=r$ for every $r$, and the formula collapses to $\mathrm{Precision}(r)=\pi r/(\pi r+(1-\pi)r)=\pi$ for all $r\in(0,1)$, the flat line at height $\pi$ identified in @thm-random-pr, as it must, since this is exactly $X_0\stackrel{d}{=}X_1$.

* **Approaching the ideal curve as $\Delta\to\infty$ (fixed $b$).** For any fixed $r\in(0,1)$, letting $\Delta\to\infty$ sends $\frac{\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\to-\infty$ and hence $\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Phi^{-1}(r)-\Delta}{\rho}\right)\to0$, giving $\mathrm{Precision}(r)\to1$ for every $r\in(0,1)$ — while $\mathrm{Precision}(1)=\pi$ always. In the limit, the curve is flat at $1$ except for a drop to $\pi$ exactly at $r=1$: the same perfect-separation Precision-Recall curve as in the equal-variance case, now reached along any fixed scale ratio $b$.

### Precision-Recall curve for the exponential case

We combine  with @thm-precision-formula to obtain a closed form for the Precision-Recall curve at a fixed prevalence $\pi=\mathbb P(Y=1)$.

:::: {#thm-exponential-pr}

# Precision-Recall curve for two exponential health-status classes

Under the model of , with rate ratio $\theta=\lambda_1/\lambda_0\in(0,1)$ and prevalence $\pi\in(0,1)$, the theoretical Precision-Recall curve has the closed-form expression
$$
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(r) = \frac{\pi}{\pi + (1-\pi)\, r^{\,1/\theta-1}}
}, \qquad r=\mathrm{Recall}(t)\in(0,1],
$$
with limiting endpoints
$$
\boxed{
\lim_{r\to0^+}\mathrm{Precision}(r) = 1
}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\boxed{
\mathrm{Precision}(1) = \pi.
}
$$
Moreover $\mathrm{Precision}(\cdot)$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,1]$.

::::

:::: {.proof-container}

::: {.proof-header onclick="toggleProof('thm-exponential-pr')"}
[▶]{#proof-arrow-thm-exponential-pr .proof-arrow} [Proof]{.proof-title}
:::

::: {#proof-content-thm-exponential-pr .proof-content}

**Step 1: Express $\mathrm{FPR}$ as a function of recall.** By , for $t\ge0$, $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=e^{-\lambda_1 t}$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=e^{-\lambda_0 t}$. Writing $r:=\mathrm{TPR}(t)=\mathrm{Recall}(t)\in(0,1]$, we have $r=e^{-\lambda_1 t}$, hence $t=-\ln(r)/\lambda_1$, and
$$
\mathrm{FPR}(t) = e^{-\lambda_0 t} = \exp\!\left(\frac{\lambda_0}{\lambda_1}\ln r\right) = r^{\lambda_0/\lambda_1} = r^{1/\theta}.
$$

**Step 2: Substitute into @thm-precision-formula.** Using $\mathrm{TPR}(t)=r$ and $\mathrm{FPR}(t)=r^{1/\theta}$,
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(t) = \frac{\pi\, r}{\pi\, r + (1-\pi)\, r^{1/\theta}} = \frac{\pi}{\pi + (1-\pi)\, r^{1/\theta - 1}},
$$
after dividing numerator and denominator by $r>0$. This is the boxed formula, now expressed purely as a function of $r$.

**Step 3: Endpoint at $r=1$.** Direct substitution gives $r^{1/\theta-1}=1$, so
$$
\mathrm{Precision}(1) = \frac{\pi}{\pi+(1-\pi)} = \pi,
$$
matching the general baseline $\lim_{t\to-\infty}\mathrm{Precision}(t)=\pi$ (obtained earlier from @lem-roc-endpoints and @thm-precision-formula).

**Step 4: Endpoint at $r\to0^+$.** Since $\theta\in(0,1)$, the exponent $1/\theta-1$ is strictly positive, so $r^{1/\theta-1}\to0$ as $r\to0^+$ — unlike the Gaussian case, this limit needs no tail asymptotics, since the power function vanishes outright. Hence
$$
\lim_{r\to0^+}\mathrm{Precision}(r) = \frac{\pi}{\pi+0} = 1.
$$

**Step 5: Monotonicity.** Since $1/\theta-1>0$, $r\mapsto r^{1/\theta-1}$ is strictly increasing on $(0,1]$, so the denominator $\pi+(1-\pi)r^{1/\theta-1}$ is strictly increasing in $r$ while the numerator $\pi$ is constant; hence $\mathrm{Precision}(r)$ is strictly decreasing on $(0,1]$.

:::

::::

**Interpretation.**

- *Recovering the random-guessing baseline.* If $\theta=1$ (i.e., $\lambda_0=\lambda_1$), the exponent $1/\theta-1$ vanishes, so $r^{1/\theta-1}\equiv1$ and the formula collapses to $\mathrm{Precision}(r)=\pi/(\pi+(1-\pi))=\pi$ for every $r\in(0,1]$ — the flat line at height $\pi$ of @thm-random-pr, as it must, since $\theta=1$ means $X_0\stackrel{d}{=}X_1$.
- *Approaching perfect separation.* As $\theta\to0^+$, the exponent $1/\theta-1\to\infty$, so $r^{1/\theta-1}\to0$ for every fixed $r\in(0,1)$ and $\mathrm{Precision}(r)\to1$ throughout the open interval, with the single unavoidable drop to $\pi$ exactly at $r=1$ — the same qualitative limiting picture as the Gaussian case's $\Delta\to\infty$ limit in `theoretical_pr_ideal`.
- *Shape versus the Gaussian case.* Both curves share the same two endpoints ($1$ at $r=0^+$, $\pi$ at $r=1$) and are strictly decreasing, but the exponential PR curve is a pure power law in $r$ with no transcendental functions involved, whereas the Gaussian one requires $\Phi,\Phi^{-1}$ — a useful contrast when illustrating that the *endpoints* of a PR curve are governed by general principles (@thm-precision-formula, @lem-roc-endpoints), while the *shape in between* is entirely model-dependent.
